item.title: Benchmarks in Leipzig
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Benchmarks in Leipzig [1], Christian Stump (Ruhr University Bochum), Veronica Calvo Cortes, and Bernd Sturmfels (Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences, Leipzig), with 46 other mathematicians, present a benchmark of 100 research-level math questions with short, known answers and report how far current frontier models get on it.

Between April 1 and May 15, 2026, a group of 49 mathematicians compiled a dataset of research-level mathematics questions with known answers. Most of the work was done during the 3-day workshop Benchmarks in Leipzig with 35 participants at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences in Leipzig, Germany. We present the resulting collection of 100 questions. We evaluated these questions in three stages: a single attempt by five state-of-the-art LLMs, followed by a 20-runs-per-model evaluation with three of these models, and finally a 3-run attempt with two heavy-thinking models. After Stage 1, 41 questions remained completely unsolved; after Stage 2, this count dropped to 16; and we concluded Stage 3 with only 2 unsolved questions. This demonstrates that the mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs are becoming impressive.

Methods

The benchmark was built by 49 mathematicians, with most of the work happening during a three-day workshop (May 11–13, 2026) with 35 participants at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences in Leipzig. The project began at the Combinatorial Coworkspace in March 2026 and runs on the ScienceBench platform, where contributors submit questions, browse and comment on each other’s, and query all the project’s models from a shared chat interface.

Each question had to meet a short set of guidelines:

  • Unique, well-defined, unguessable answer: the answer is short and checkable, and a reader who guesses repeatedly without working out the details should have no realistic chance of getting it right.
  • Grounded in public research, but beyond it: questions build on existing, publicly accessible work but go past what a paper itself states, and the solution cannot depend on non-public results.
  • Hard to guess in practice was the tricky part: several submissions turned out to have only a few possible answers, and were reworked or dropped.

Submissions then went through an audit. Before any model attempted a question, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro checked it against the guidelines. Every contributor could see all questions alongside the models’ answers and solutions, and comparing submissions against model-generated solutions led to 12 reformulated questions and 3 removed from the set. The final 100 questions skew heavily toward the contributors’ own fields (Table 1, the cover): 36 in algebraic geometry, then algebraic combinatorics (22), matroid theory (18), representation theory (15), and enumerative combinatorics (15), with a long tail of smaller areas. The authors generated that area breakdown with Claude Opus 4.7 and then verified it by hand.

Results

The 100 questions were run through three evaluation stages, with a question counted as “solved” if at least one model run produced the correct answer:

  • Stage 1 (single attempt): five project-active models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Grok 4.3) and their immediate predecessors each got one try per question during submission.
  • Stage 2 (20 runs): Surge AI queried three of the models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7) 20 times on each question.
  • Stage 3 (heavy thinking): GPT-5.5 Pro with Extended Thinking (3 runs, via ChatGPT) and Gemini 3.1 Pro Deep Think (3 runs, via Surge AI).

The unsolved count shrinks across the three stages: 41 after Stage 1, 16 after Stage 2, and just 2 after Stage 3. The per-stage detail:

  • Single attempt favors one model: GPT-5.5 solved 44 of 100 on one try, the next best (Gemini 3.1 Pro) managed 15, and Grok 4.3 just 6 (Table 2). Predecessor models trailed their successors in most cases.
  • More samples close most of the gap: with 20 runs each, GPT-5.5 solved 75 of 100 (52% of its 2,000 attempts correct), Gemini 3.1 Pro 40 (20%), and Claude Opus 4.7 44 (15%) (Table 3).
  • Heavy-thinking modes close almost all of it: GPT-5.5 Pro with Extended Thinking answered every one of its 300 runs, got 79% right, and solved 88 of 100, while Gemini 3.1 Pro Deep Think solved 56 (Table 4).
  • First-solved breakdown: 59 questions were first cracked in Stage 1, 25 more in Stage 2, 14 in Stage 3, leaving 2 unsolved.

Per-question consistency differs by model (Table 6). GPT-5.5 is bimodal: it got every attempt wrong on 25 questions and every attempt right on 27, with relatively few in between. For the other two models, correct answers spread more thinly across the 20 runs, with more questions solved on only a handful of attempts.

My Notes

  • The benchmark already saturates at the top: the abstract calls the results a sign that “the mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs are becoming impressive,” but the body’s first key finding is blunter. The exercise-style recipe (questions drawn from published research with a short checkable answer) has “reached its limits” for the best models, which solve almost all of them: GPT-5.5 Pro with Extended Thinking got 88 of the 100 (Table 4). The method still separates weaker models, but the limit is difficulty rather than supply: more questions of the same kind would not be hard enough to measure the frontier.

  • The solve count overstates repeatable ability: a question counts as solved on one correct run out of twenty, so the headline totals treat a reliable answer and a one-in-twenty fluke the same. The per-question distribution (Table 6) shows how far apart the two can be. GPT-5.5 is bimodal: wrong on all 20 runs for 25 questions and right on all 20 for 27, with little in between. Across the three models, many solved questions were answered correctly on only one to four of the twenty runs, so much of the solve count rests on inconsistent, sometimes lucky, results.

  • The questions are built to resist contamination: three features keep these question and answer pairs out of the models’ training data. They are new, written in April and May 2026, after the evaluated checkpoints were frozen (Gemini 3.1 Pro shipped March 17, GPT-5.5 April 23), so the pairs did not exist when the models were trained. They are unpublished by design, each made to go beyond what would fit in a paper, so the specific question and answer are not online to scrape. And the answer key was shown to neither the models nor the other contributors. A model saw only the question. The one thing this does not rule out, deliberately, is the models having learned the public results the solutions build on, but that is the capability being tested rather than leakage.

References

  1. Stump, C., Calvo Cortes, V., Sturmfels, B., and 46 others. “Benchmarks in Leipzig: A Collection of Questions in Research-Level Mathematics.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.05818), June 4, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05818

Related Posts

  • Mapping Benchmark Creation and Saturation in AI: the create-then-saturate pattern this benchmark already shows, a fresh research-math set nearly solved by frontier models.
  • Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search: the verification-backed alternative, settling open problems with machine-checked Lean proofs rather than grading against a known answer.
  • An OpenAI Model Disproves a Discrete-Geometry Conjecture: a single high-profile instance of the research-math capability this benchmark measures across 100 questions.
  • Math Is AGI: Carina Hong on Axiom and Formal Reasoning: the argument that trustworthy LLM math needs a deterministic verifier, relevant when a solve can be a one-in-twenty fluke.
  • The Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics: names training-data contamination and unverifiable AI math claims as threats that this benchmark’s post-cutoff, hidden-answer design is built to resist.

item.title: Unlocking Scientific Intuition and Reasoning at Digital Speed
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Pushmeet Kohli, Vice President of Science and Strategic Initiatives at Google DeepMind, writes in Dædalus that AI is the latest instrument in a lineage running from the telescope and microscope: a lens that supplies “machine intuition” for making sense of scientific complexity [1]. The essay walks through biology, materials science, and mathematics before turning to agentic systems that generate their own hypotheses.

The essay’s abstract:

Throughout history, scientific progress has been defined by the tools we build to extend our perception. Today, artificial intelligence stands as our newest instrument, not merely as a computational engine but as a revolutionary lens for deciphering the nature of reality. Drawing on my research journey at Google DeepMind, this essay explores how scientists are deploying AI to overcome the hardest “root node” bottlenecks in science. By applying machine intuition, we are uncovering breakthroughs across biology, materials science, and mathematics, from solving the grand challenge of protein folding with AlphaFold to charting new universes of stable materials with GNoME. The essay concludes by reflecting on the transition toward open-ended, agentic AI systems that actively generate novel hypotheses and their implications for the nature of scientific inquiry. We are evolving from the solvers of intricate puzzles into the architects of profound questions, embarking on the most exciting journey of discovery ever undertaken.

The essay is a first-person tour of DeepMind’s AI-for-science program, structured as deep dives into three fields. What it covers:

  • The thesis: AI extends the telescope-microscope-computer lineage by supplying “machine intuition,” a learned strategy for finding structure in data too vast for human perception. It targets two limits on inquiry, the scale of what we try to understand and the speed at which we can test ideas, and selects “root node” problems: foundational bottlenecks that experts agree won’t fall to existing methods within a decade.
  • Biology: AlphaFold 2 solved the fifty-year grand challenge of protein folding to atomic accuracy in 2020 [2], and the AlphaFold database now holds structures for more than 200 million proteins used by three million researchers across 190 countries [3]. AlphaFold 3 extended this to how proteins bind DNA, RNA, and other molecules [4], while AlphaMissense classifies DNA variants as benign or harmful [5]. The essay also credits outside work: EVEscape for forward-looking vaccine design [6], David Baker’s from-scratch protein design (a shared 2024 Nobel in Chemistry) [7], the AI-found antibiotic halicin [8], and a petabyte-scale map of a human brain circuit [9].
  • Materials science: GNoME learned to approximate the rules of quantum chemistry and returned 2.2 million candidate materials, 380,000 of them predicted stable, which the essay puts at roughly eight hundred years of progress in a single day [10]. The candidates still have to be synthesized and tested, where self-driving labs are beginning to help. Related projects include real-time control of fusion-reactor plasma with EPFL (École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne) [11] and pulling rare signals from Large Hadron Collider data [12].
  • Mathematics: AlphaProof proves statements in the formal language Lean, where a result is machine-checkable, and with AlphaGeometry it reached silver-medal level at the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad. Gemini Deep Think reached gold in 2025 [13]. The essay is candid that Olympiad problems are not research, and points to AlphaEvolve, tested on more than fifty open math problems, where it matched the best known solution in three-quarters of cases and improved on it in a fifth [14], as the closer analog to discovery.
  • The forward look: the essay closes on agentic systems that generate their own hypotheses, a shift from “solvers of intricate puzzles” to “architects of profound questions.”

item.title: Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search [1] (arXiv preprint, May 2026), George Tsoukalas, Anton Kovsharov, Sergey Shirobokov, and 15 colleagues at Google DeepMind and Aarhus University — with Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri as corresponding authors — report the first large-scale evaluation of LLM-driven formal proof search on open mathematical problems.

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly excel at mathematical reasoning, but their unreliability limits their utility in mathematics research. A mitigation is using LLMs to generate formal proofs in languages like Lean. We perform the first large-scale evaluation of this method’s ability to solve open problems. Our most capable agent autonomously resolved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems at the per-problem cost of a few hundred dollars, proved 44/492 OEIS conjectures, and is being deployed in combinatorics, optimization, graph theory, algebraic geometry, and quantum optics research. A basic agent alternating LLM-based generation with Lean-based verification replicated the Erdős successes but proved costlier on the hardest problems. These findings demonstrate the power of AI-aided formal proof search and shed light on the agent designs that enable it.

Methods

AlphaProof Nexus is a framework for agents that query two things in a loop: a frontier LLM that proposes mathematics, and the Lean compiler that checks it. In Lean, definitions, theorems, and proofs are all mechanically verified code. A proof is built from tactics, elementary steps the compiler runs one at a time while tracking the goals still left to prove, and it is complete only when no goals remain. Lean also has a sorry tactic that closes any goal while still passing the type-checker, so proving a theorem reduces to a concrete coding task: rewrite the file until it compiles with no sorry left.

The agent’s input is a proof sketch: a Lean file holding the target theorem, the definitions and library imports it depends on, and sorry where the proof should go. The mathematician can add natural-language context and domain knowledge encoded in Lean, and marks which parts of the file the agent may edit, with EVOLVE-BLOCK regions where it can introduce helper lemmas, definitions, and proof steps, and EVOLVE-VALUE regions enclosing parameters whose values it may change. On success the agent returns a sorry-free proof.

The paper builds four agents on this framework and tests them in four combinations:

  • (A) Basic generate-and-verify. A set of prover subagents run independently with no shared state. Each is a “Ralph loop”: a sequence of episodes, where an episode is a multi-turn Gemini 3.1 Pro inference loop that reasons step by step and edits the sketch with a search-and-replace tool. After each turn the subagent compiles the sketch. A Lean error message becomes the instruction for the next turn. If an episode ends with a sorry still in the file, the subagent writes a comment summarizing what it learned, and that annotated sketch seeds the next episode.
  • (B) Basic plus AlphaProof. The prover can hand an unproved goal to AlphaProof, DeepMind’s reinforcement-learning prover for Olympiad-level Lean. AlphaProof returns a proof, which is substituted straight into the sketch, a disproof showing the goal is false, or a failure message. Disproofs and failures are fed back into the prover’s prompt.
  • (C) Basic plus evolution. Prover subagents draw from and contribute to a shared population of validated sketches, in the style of DeepMind’s AlphaEvolve. Formal proof is pass-or-fail, which leaves an evolutionary search nothing to climb, so a pool of cheaper Gemini 3.0 Flash rater subagents ranks sketches by plausibility, clarity, and novelty: an LLM critic compares them in pairwise matches, the results become Elo scores, and a selection rule from Monte Carlo tree search (P-UCB, which favors high-scoring sketches while still exploring less-tried ones) decides which to evolve next.
  • (D) Full-featured. Combines AlphaProof and evolutionary search, and is the agent used for the paper’s main results.

A validator checks every result before it counts, confirming that the final sketch compiles and that the agent did not quietly weaken the theorem statement to make the proof easier.

Results

The evaluation covers 353 open Erdős problems and 492 conjectures from the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS), with a focused cost comparison run on six Erdős instances. The metric is solve rate against mean inference cost in dollars, swept over independent attempts. The prover is Gemini 3.1 Pro and the rater Gemini 3.0 Flash. Reported costs exclude AlphaProof’s own inference (estimated around $60 per problem), which the authors note does not change the comparison.

The findings:

  • Nine of 353 open Erdős problems solved by the full-featured agent (D), including two that had been open for 56 years, at a few hundred dollars per problem.
  • Forty-four of 492 OEIS conjectures proved.
  • The basic agent (A) solved all nine Erdős problems too, at higher cost on the hardest ones. On most problems (A) or (B) sat on the cost–performance Pareto frontier, and the full-featured (D) pulled ahead only on the hardest, such as Erdős #125.
  • Already in use in active research across optimization theory, graph theory, algebraic geometry, additive combinatorics, and quantum optics.

My Notes

  • The base model matters more than the orchestration: the basic generate-and-verify loop (A) solved all nine Erdős problems on its own. Adding AlphaProof (B) mostly matched it within the margin of error, and the full-featured agent (D) beat them only on the hardest instances (#138 and #125, 2–5x cheaper there) while running about twice as expensive on the rest. Standalone AlphaProof and versions of (A) built on smaller Gemini models solved nothing. The capability comes from the frontier prover, not the evolutionary machinery around it, because the Lean compiler already supplies a hard correctness signal. Co-Scientist [2] is the opposite case: with no compiler to check its hypotheses, its Elo tournament is the only quality signal it has, so the same machinery that is optional here becomes essential.

  • Humans still formalize the problem and digest the proof: the agent only starts once someone has written the conjecture as a Lean theorem, and its output is a machine-checked proof that still has to be read back out (“deformalized”) and understood. It is the split Terence Tao named: generation and verification race ahead while digestion lags. It also revives the older question of what mathematicians are for once a machine can write the proof.

  • Known answers versus open problems: the Leipzig benchmark [3] graded models on 100 research-level questions that already had known answers, leaving only two unsolved after three rounds. This paper instead targets open problems with no known answer, where a result counts only when the Lean compiler accepts the proof.

  • A price tag on open problems: a few hundred dollars to settle a question open for decades makes attempting a conjecture a budgeting decision. Progress now has a unit cost, so you can buy more of it, like the broader automation of AI R&D. The bottleneck remains human bandwidth: formalizing the problems and digesting the proofs.

References

  1. Tsoukalas, George, Kovsharov, Anton, Shirobokov, Sergey, Surina, Anja, Firsching, Moritz, Bérczi, Gergely, Ruiz, Francisco J. R., Suggala, Arun, Wagner, Adam Zsolt, Wieser, Eric, Yu, Lei, Huang, Aja, Horváth, Miklós Z., Ferrauiolo, Andrew, Michalewski, Henryk, Grosu, Codrut, Hubert, Thomas, Balog, Matej, Kohli, Pushmeet, and Chaudhuri, Swarat. “Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.22763), May 21, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763
  2. Gottweis, Juraj, Weng, Wei-Hung, Daryin, Alexander, and 48 co-authors. “Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist.” Nature (DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y), May 19, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y
  3. Balakin, Andrei, Bóna, Miklós, Brandenburg, Marie-Charlotte, and 46 co-authors. “Benchmarks in Leipzig.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.05818), June 4, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05818

Related Posts

  • An OpenAI Model Disproves a Discrete-Geometry Conjecture: the informal counterpart, an Erdős conjecture settled by a general model and checked by a human committee rather than a compiler.
  • Even Experts Are Surprised by AI’s Latest ‘Vibe-Mathing’ Advance: another AI result on a long-open math problem, with the value in a transferable technique rather than the single proof.
  • Math Is AGI: Carina Hong on Axiom and Formal Reasoning: the same bet that formal, machine-checkable proof is the path for AI mathematics.
  • The Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics: the governance counterpart, asking for human oversight of AI in mathematical research.

item.title: An OpenAI Model Disproves a Discrete-Geometry Conjecture
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

OpenAI [1] reports that an internal, general-purpose reasoning model resolved a longstanding question about the planar unit distance problem, which Paul Erdős first posed in 1946.

The Unit Distance Problem

Placing points in the plane, at most how many pairs can be exactly distance 1 apart? Put concretely: scatter pins on a board and join every pair exactly an inch apart with a rigid one-inch rod, then count the rods. The count seems like it should climb freely as you add pins, but the plane is unforgiving: once a few pins are fixed, there are only so many spots left where a new pin can be an inch from several others at once.

Erdős conjectured an upper bound of on this maximum, where the in the exponent is a term that shrinks to 0 as grows. The best construction, a rescaled square grid, reaches , whose excess shrinks the same way, only slightly faster than linear, and was widely believed to be essentially optimal. From the opposite side, the maximum is known to be no more than , an upper bound Spencer, Szemerédi, and Trotter proved in 1984 [2].

What OpenAI Reports

  • The result: the conjecture was an upper bound, and the model disproved it from below. For infinitely many , it constructs point configurations with at least unit-distance pairs for a fixed exponent that does not shrink with . That construction is a stronger lower bound, not a new upper bound, and it beats the old record by a factor of about , a genuine power of rather than a vanishing one, which is the polynomial improvement that breaks the conjectured ceiling. The proof shows only that some such exists. A subsequent refinement by Princeton mathematician Will Sawin pins it at [3]. This disproves the conjecture without settling the problem. Writing for the largest possible number of unit-distance pairs, the best bounds now known are , and the exact growth rate between them is still unknown.
  • The method: the proof replaces the Gaussian integers behind Erdős’s original lower bound with deeper objects from algebraic number theory, using infinite class field towers and Golod–Shafarevich theory to bring number theory to bear on an elementary geometry question.
  • Verification: a group of external mathematicians checked the proof [4] and wrote a companion paper [5] explaining the argument and its significance, which OpenAI says “paints a substantially richer picture than the original solution alone.” OpenAI describes this as an early glimpse of AI–human collaboration: the model generated and the proof was checkable, but the richer understanding came only with the second, human-written paper, the generation-and-digestion split Terence Tao has described.

My Notes

  • A general model found a hidden cross-domain connection: an elementary plane-geometry question fell to class field towers, machinery number theorists knew well but had no reason to point at distances in the plane. The notable thing is not that a 1946 conjecture fell but that the connection existed at all, and that a general reasoning model, run over a set of Erdős problems rather than scaffolded for proof search, found it. Whether the same machine intuition transfers to problems where no such hidden connection exists is the open question. The Leiden Declaration’s call for human oversight reads differently once the proof is checkable line by line.

References

  1. OpenAI. “An OpenAI Model Has Disproved a Central Conjecture in Discrete Geometry.” May 20, 2026. https://openai.com/index/model-disproves-discrete-geometry-conjecture/
  2. Spencer, Joel, Szemerédi, Endre, and Trotter, William T. “Unit distances in the Euclidean plane.” In Graph Theory and Combinatorics (Béla Bollobás, ed.), London: Academic Press, 1984, pp. 293–308.
  3. Sawin, Will. “An explicit lower bound for the unit distance problem.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.20579), May 20, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579
  4. OpenAI. The model’s proof of the unit distance result (PDF). https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/74c24085-19b0-4534-9c90-465b8e29ad73/unit-distance-proof.pdf
  5. Companion remarks on the proof, by the external mathematicians who checked it (PDF). https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/74c24085-19b0-4534-9c90-465b8e29ad73/unit-distance-remarks.pdf

  • Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search: the formal counterpart, closing open Erdős problems with machine-checked Lean proofs instead of an informal proof a human committee verifies.

item.title: Robin: A Multi-Agent System That Ran the Whole Discovery Loop
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In A multi-agent system for automating scientific discovery [1] (Nature, May 2026), Ali Essam Ghareeb and Benjamin Chang (co-first authors), jointly supervised by Andrew D. White, Michaela M. Hinks, and Samuel G. Rodriques, with nine co-authors from FutureHouse, the University of Oxford, and Fordham University, introduce Robin, a system of bird-named agents that runs an experimental-biology project end to end: it reads the literature, proposes hypotheses, designs experiments, and analyzes the data that comes back.

Scientific discovery is driven by the iterative process of observation, hypothesis generation, experimentation, and data analysis. Despite recent advancements in applying artificial intelligence to biology, no system has yet automated all these stages. Here, we introduce Robin, the first multi-agent system capable of fully automating both hypothesis generation and data analysis for experimental biology. By integrating literature search agents with data analysis agents, Robin can generate hypotheses, propose experiments, interpret experimental results, and generate updated hypotheses, achieving a semi-autonomous approach to scientific discovery. By applying this system, we were able to identify promising therapeutic candidates for dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD), the major cause of blindness in the developed world. Robin proposed enhancing retinal pigment epithelium phagocytosis as a therapeutic strategy, and identified and confirmed in vitro efficacy for ripasudil and KL001. Ripasudil is a clinically-used Rho kinase (ROCK) inhibitor that has never previously been proposed for treating dAMD. To elucidate the mechanism of ripasudil-induced upregulation of phagocytosis, Robin then proposed and analyzed a follow-up RNA-seq experiment, which revealed upregulation of ABCA1, a lipid efflux pump and possible novel target. All hypotheses, experimental directions, data analyses, and data figures in the main text of this report were produced by Robin. As the first AI system to autonomously discover and validate novel therapeutic candidates within an iterative lab-in-the-loop framework, Robin establishes a new paradigm for AI-driven scientific discovery.

Methods

Robin coordinates three specialized bird-named agents, with a human running the wet-lab steps in between. It is semi-autonomous by design: humans execute the experiments and review the ranked candidates, and every hit is treated as a hypothesis that still needs standard pre-clinical and clinical validation.

  • The agents are split by job. Crow and Falcon are literature-search agents — Crow runs concise searches, Falcon deep ones — with access to the scientific literature, clinical-trial reports, and the Open Targets Platform. Finch is the data-analysis agent, writing and running its own code in a Jupyter notebook to analyze flow-cytometry and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data. Robin is not a single model: Crow and Falcon run on OpenAI’s o4-mini to synthesize what they retrieve, while Anthropic’s Claude 3.7 Sonnet serves as the ranking judge and as Finch’s base model.
  • The loop. Given only a disease name, Robin uses Crow to propose candidate mechanisms, each paired with an in vitro model to test it, ranks those reports, and runs the top one as its assay (a lab test that measures a specific biological activity). Falcon then evaluates drug candidates, ranked by the strength of the scientific rationale, the pharmacological profile, and the quality of the supporting literature. Ranking is pairwise: the LLM judge compares reports two at a time (round-robin for 25 or fewer, otherwise 300 sampled pairs), and a Bradley-Terry-Luce model — the standard way to turn pairwise win/loss records into a single strength score per item — produces the ranking. A human runs the top picks in the lab, Finch analyzes the returned data, and Robin interprets the result to seed the next round.
  • Consensus over many analysis runs. Because reading biological data is ambiguous and the agents are stochastic, Finch runs several independent analysis trajectories and a meta-analysis reconciles them into a consensus before Robin acts on it.
  • Throughput. Robin analyzed 551 papers in about 30 minutes against an estimated 540 hours for a human, roughly a 200-fold reduction over running the workflow by hand.

Results

The team pointed Robin at dry AMD as a proof of concept.

  • Robin picked a phagocytosis assay and ran the screen. From an initial review of 151 papers it proposed boosting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytosis and chose that assay over four alternatives (Figure 2a), then read about 400 more papers to rank 30 drug candidates. The assay doses cells, adds pH-sensitive (pHrodo) beads, and reads uptake by flow cytometry (2b); Finch wrote the gating code to isolate live single cells (2c–e) and scored each drug’s fold-change in fluorescence against a DMSO (solvent) control, where the Rho-kinase (ROCK) inhibitor Y-27632 came out significant (2f). Plainly: the cells that keep the retina clean normally swallow up debris; Robin bet that helping them do more of it would treat the disease, built a dish test for that swallowing, and found a compound (Y-27632) that boosted it.
  • A follow-up RNA-seq experiment pointed at ABCA1. To explain why Y-27632 worked, Robin proposed sequencing treated RPE cells. Finch’s differential-expression analysis found a 3-fold upregulation of ABCA1, a lipid efflux pump (Figure 3b), agreed across most of its analysis trajectories (3c), with gene-ontology (GO) enrichment in actin-filament organization, small-GTPase signaling, and autophagy (3d) — consistent with a cytoskeletal route to the phagocytic boost. Plainly: to learn why that compound helped, Robin read which genes the treated cells switched on, and a fat-transport gene called ABCA1 stood out — hinting that the cells’ internal scaffolding is what changed.
  • Ripasudil outperformed Y-27632 and validated in primary cells. In a second round Robin proposed ripasudil, a ROCK inhibitor approved for glaucoma in Japan and never before proposed for dAMD (Figure 4a). It raised phagocytosis 1.89-fold over DMSO (4b) and was more potent than Y-27632 in a dose-response (4c). Re-screening in stem-cell-derived primary human RPE confirmed both as hits, ripasudil again the stronger (4d–e), alongside KL001, a circadian-clock modulator. Plainly: next Robin proposed ripasudil, an existing glaucoma drug, which worked even better and kept working in real human cells — as did KL001, a drug that acts on the body clock.
  • Ablations confirmed the literature search mattered. Stripping the retrieval out from under Crow and Falcon — leaving the same o4-mini model to answer on its own — drove hallucinated references from 0% to 44.5%, and OpenAI’s Deep Research, given the same prompt, generated candidates that produced no hits in the assay [1]. Plainly: when the same model had to work without Robin’s literature tools, it invented fake references and its drug picks failed — the careful reading was what made the difference.

My Notes

  • Robin and Co-Scientist refine hypotheses in opposite directions. Google’s Co-Scientist [2] improves its hypotheses internally and scales their quality with more test-time compute, but the quality signal is the model scoring its own debates — an internal-consistency measure, with experimental validation left to humans. Robin improves them externally instead, feeding Finch’s analysis of real wet-lab data back into the next round. The improvement is anchored to different things: for Co-Scientist, a self-evaluated score; for Robin, experimental results. By the Robin paper’s own framing, analyzing those results and re-hypothesizing on them is the step prior systems, Co-Scientist among them, did not automate [1].

  • Grounding the literature search is what mattered. Robin’s own ablations are the clearest evidence: strip the retrieval out and the references hallucinate, swap in a general-purpose research agent and the drug picks all miss in the assay. Co-Scientist relied on the same move: its Reflection agent called external search to hold implausible hypotheses down. Two independently built systems converging on literature-grounded retrieval over a bare general model is the quietly useful part.

References

  2. Gottweis, Juraj, Weng, Wei-Hung, Daryin, Alexander, Tu, Tao, et al. “Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist.” Nature (DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y), May 19, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y

  • MAST: A Failure Taxonomy for Multi-Agent Systems: the failure modes, including weak verification and inter-agent misalignment, that Robin’s consensus trajectories, human-in-the-loop checks, and retrieval grounding are built to avoid.
  • Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies: treats the agent topology itself as the thing to optimize, where Robin instead fixes a hand-designed topology and grounds it in wet-lab feedback.
  • Are AI Systems About to Start Building Themselves?: the case for automating the research pipeline, with Robin a data point on the science side that automates hypothesis search and analysis while humans run the lab.

item.title: Co-Scientist: Gemini Agents That Generate and Rank Hypotheses
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist [1] (Nature, May 2026), Juraj Gottweis, Wei-Hung Weng, Alexander Daryin, Tao Tu, and five other co-first authors, with senior authors including Vivek Natarajan, Demis Hassabis, James Manyika, Yossi Matias, and Pushmeet Kohli, and roughly 50 co-authors across Google DeepMind, Google Research, Google Cloud AI Research, Stanford University School of Medicine, Houston Methodist, and Imperial College London, introduce Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based system that proposes research hypotheses and ranks them in a tournament that improves the survivors.

Scientific discovery is driven by scientists generating novel hypotheses for complex problems that undergo rigorous experimental validation. To augment this process, we introduce Co-Scientist, a multi-agent AI system built on Gemini for structured scientific thinking and hypothesis generation. Co-Scientist aims to help scientists discover new original knowledge. Conditioned on their research objectives and prior scientific evidence, it formulates demonstrably novel research hypotheses for experimental verification. The system’s design involves agents continuously generating, critiquing and refining hypotheses accelerated by scaling test-time compute. Key contributions include: (1) a multi-agent architecture with an asynchronous task execution framework for flexible compute scaling; (2) a tournament evolution process for self-improving hypotheses generation. Automated evaluations show continued benefits of test-time compute scaling, improving hypothesis quality over time. While general purpose, we focus the validation in three biomedical applications: drug repurposing, novel target discovery, and explaining mechanisms of anti-microbial resistance. Specifically, Co-Scientist helped identify new drug repurposing candidates and synergistic combination therapies for acute myeloid leukemia, which were validated through in vitro experiments. These real-world validations demonstrate the potential of Co-Scientist to accelerate scientific discovery and usher in an era of AI empowered scientists.

Methods

Co-Scientist is a compound, multi-agent system built on Gemini, run as a “scientist in the loop”: a researcher states a goal in natural language, sets constraints, and can steer the search or seed hypotheses as it works. The system generates and ranks hypotheses, but the experimental validation stays with people: every proposal passes human expert review and wet-lab assays before it is confirmed.

  • Six specialized agents under a supervisor. A Supervisor agent parses the goal and assigns six worker agents (Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity, and Meta-review) to an asynchronous task queue, all sharing a persistent context memory. The agents are not separate models: they all run on the same base LLM (Gemini 2.0 here) and differ only by their prompts, and the framework is model-agnostic. Every hypothesis must meet default criteria: plausibility, novelty, testability, and safety.
  • Grounding and critique. The Generation agent drafts hypotheses from literature search and simulated scientific debate. The Reflection agent then reviews them as a peer reviewer would, and its access to web search and specialized AI models is what kept hallucinated, implausible hypotheses down.
  • Fitness is winning debates. Hypotheses are scored by an internal Elo rating — the chess-style score that ranks competitors, here hypotheses, by who wins pairwise matchups. The Ranking agent stages those matchups as multi-turn scientific debates (single-turn for lower-ranked pairs), judged on correctness, novelty, and testability. A new hypothesis enters at an Elo of 1200 and climbs or falls by its record. The Proximity agent clusters similar hypotheses so the debates pit close rivals against each other.
  • Evolution reproduces rather than overwrites. The Evolution agent builds new hypotheses from the top-ranked ones: combining the strongest parts of several (the crossover analog), spinning off variants inspired by one or more parents, regrounding them in fresh literature, simplifying them, or forcing deliberately divergent “out-of-the-box” ideas (the mutation analog). It never edits a hypothesis in place, so strong parents survive and every offspring has to earn its own Elo back in the tournament.
  • It improves without retraining. A Meta-review agent distills recurring weaknesses from the reviews and debates and appends that feedback to every agent’s prompt on the next round, so the system learns by updating its context rather than its weights, with no fine-tuning or reinforcement learning. An asynchronous framework lets it spend more test-time compute on a goal, with the Supervisor tracking progress through periodic summary statistics and deciding when a run hits a terminal state. There is no convergence threshold: quality (Elo) never saturated in the paper’s runs, so they ended on a compute budget rather than because the system stopped improving.

Results

The paper validates Co-Scientist with automated benchmarks and end-to-end wet-lab experiments in three biomedical areas, all run with experts in the loop. [1]

  • Quality climbs with test-time compute. Across 203 research goals, both the average and best Elo ratings rose the longer the system reasoned, with no sign of saturation.
  • Beats frontier reasoning models. On 15 expert-curated goals, Co-Scientist’s Elo eventually surpassed Gemini 2.0 Pro and Flash Thinking, OpenAI o1 and o3-mini-high, and DeepSeek R1.
  • Experts preferred its output. On 11 goals, Co-Scientist scored an average preference rank of 2.36 and novelty and impact ratings of 3.64 and 3.09 out of 5, and was the top pick of all four LLM judges.
  • AML drug repurposing. Co-Scientist generated repurposing hypotheses across a curated list of 2,300 approved drugs spanning 34 cancer types. After expert oncologists reviewed and ranked its predictions, five candidates were tested in vitro, and three (binimetinib, pacritinib, cerivastatin) inhibited acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cell viability. Binimetinib, approved for metastatic melanoma, reached a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50, the dose that cuts cell survival in half, so lower means more potent) as low as 2 nM in all AML lines but NOMO-1, while leaving a non-leukemia control line largely unharmed.
  • Novel single-agent candidates. With no prior preclinical evidence or human feedback, Co-Scientist proposed three wholly new picks: nanvuranlat, KIRA6, and leflunomide. KIRA6, which blocks a cellular stress sensor (the enzyme IRE1α), had an 18-fold safety margin: it killed the stem-cell-like KG-1a leukemia cells at one-eighteenth the dose that affected healthy control cells (an IC50 of 10 nM against 180 nM).
  • Synergistic combinations. Co-Scientist also proposed multi-drug regimens, and of seven it suggested, the two- and three-drug combinations were mostly synergistic in one leukemia line (MOLM-13), meaning the drugs together killed more cells than the sum of each alone, while the harder-to-treat KG-1a line responded inconsistently.
  • Liver fibrosis and antimicrobial resistance. In lab-grown mini-livers (hepatic organoids), Co-Scientist proposed three epigenetic targets (genes that switch other genes on or off), and drugs against two of them reduced scarring without harming the tissue (one, vorinostat, is already an approved cancer drug). For antimicrobial resistance, it worked out in about two days how a family of mobile DNA elements that ferry resistance genes between bacteria (cf-PICIs) jump across species, by borrowing the tail proteins of different viruses, matching an unpublished experiment that was running at the same time.

My Notes

  • Both Nature papers point to the same lesson: grounding beats the raw model. Co-Scientist’s own ablation found that giving the Reflection agent access to external search tools is what prevented hallucinated, implausible hypotheses [1] — the gains came from disciplined literature retrieval rather than a bigger base model. FutureHouse’s Robin [2], in Nature the same week, reached the comparable conclusion automating discovery for macular degeneration. Two independently built systems converging on the same point is the part worth remembering.

  • The Elo curve is self-evaluated. It is scored by the same model that generates the hypotheses, so a rising Elo means later hypotheses beat earlier ones in the model’s own debates — an internal-consistency signal that can optimize for what the judge likes rather than what is true. The only anchor to real quality is the small human-expert correlation on 11 goals. The wet-lab hits are the harder evidence.

References

  1. D., Penadés, José R., Peltz, Gary, Matias, Yossi, Manyika, James, Hassabis, Demis, Xu, Yunhan, Kohli, Pushmeet, Pawlosky, Annalisa, Karthikesalingam, Alan, Natarajan, Vivek. “Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist.” Nature (DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y), May 19, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y
  2. Ghareeb, Ali Essam, Chang, Benjamin, Mitchener, Ludovico, et al. “A multi-agent system for automating scientific discovery.” Nature (DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10652-y), May 19, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10652-y

Related Posts

  • EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers: the same paradigm behind Co-Scientist’s Evolution agent, an LLM run as the evolutionary operator over a population with no gradients or retraining.
  • Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning: the lens that classifies Co-Scientist’s self-improvement as extrinsic, since its Elo objective, agent roles, and stopping rule are all human-designed.
  • A Deep Learning Approach to Antibiotic Discovery: the AI-drug-discovery precedent, where a model found a novel antibiotic later confirmed in the lab, as Co-Scientist’s AML repurposing candidates were validated in vitro.

item.title: AutoScientist: Automating the Science of Model Training
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Adaption’s launch post introduces AutoScientist, a system that automates the training of fine-tuned models.

  • The company: Adaption (also styled Adaption Labs) is privately held, based in San Francisco, and co-founded by Sara Hooker, with 11–50 staff. Its mission is “the future of Adaptable Intelligence”: models that keep adapting to new conditions instead of being retrained from scratch.
  • What it does: AutoScientist automates the training-and-alignment loop, co-optimizing the data and the recipe together and self-improving over a limited number of past runs until quality converges. It targets the usual failure modes of training outside a frontier lab: catastrophic forgetting, overfitting on thin data, and conflicting training signals.
  • The claim: all win rates are scored on Adaption’s own in-house, domain-specialized evaluations. The headline is that AutoScientist beats fine-tuning configured by the lab’s own AI research staff by an average of 35% across runs, with the aggregate win rate going from 48% (staff-configured) to 64% (AutoScientist). Datasets run 5K–100K on the architectures Together AI offers, and AutoScientist is free for 30 days.

The per-vertical view uses a different baseline, the original un-fine-tuned model, and AutoScientist beats it on all eight verticals: it scores 59–69% against 31–41% for the original model, with the widest gap in Finance (31% to 69%).

One caveat on reading these numbers: the post describes “consistent gains against the base model,” yet its per-vertical chart scores that original model at about 35%, not the 50% a model scores against itself. What the win rate is measured against is left unclear, and the aggregate chart (48% vs 64%) and the per-vertical chart (about 35% vs 65%) do not share a baseline.

Related Posts

  • Are AI Systems About to Start Building Themselves? — Jack Clark’s survey of the public evidence on automating AI R&D (coding loops, kernel design, fine-tuning automation). AutoScientist’s recipe search is one well-scoped instance of that category.
  • Recursive Superintelligence’s $4B Bet on Self-Improving AI — a far larger wager on automating AI research itself, the maximalist version of the same self-improvement idea.
  • AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions — survey evidence on how far AI-R&D automation has actually gotten, a calibration check on AutoScientist’s 35% win-rate claim.

item.title: Mira Murati on Interaction Models and Keeping Humans in the Loop
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

At Bloomberg Tech 2026 in San Francisco, Bloomberg’s Emily Chang interviewed Mira Murati, co-founder and CEO of Thinking Machines Lab, the AI lab she started in February 2025 after leaving OpenAI, where she had been CTO. The 28-minute conversation covers the lab’s first public bet (interaction models), her account of the November 2023 OpenAI board crisis, the war for AI talent, and why she’s building toward human-AI collaboration rather than the autonomy-first path most labs are racing down.

With the help of AI, I’ve built an enriched transcript at the bottom of this post — the video’s auto-captions, reorganized into chapters with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor’s-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for details.

A few takeaways worth jumping to:

  • Interaction models are an interface bet: continuous, time-based models that take in audio, text, and video in 20-millisecond chunks, rather than the turn-based prompt-then-wait loop of today’s models.
  • She bets on collaboration over autonomy: she grants the autonomy-first path is the faster way to advance AI, and chooses instead to bring machine intelligence closer to human intent.
  • She casts November 2023 as a governance failure: her one regret is not pausing on the transition plan; she leaves the question of whether removing Altman was right unanswered.
  • “Humans in the loop” as a tandem bike: both riders pedaling, both hands on the wheel, with alignment offered as a byproduct of collaboration.

YouTube chapters (jump to the enriched transcript below, or watch on YouTube):

  • 0:00:00 — What interaction models are: continuous, not turn-based (YouTube)
  • 0:02:45 — The bet: human-AI collaboration over pure autonomy (YouTube)
  • 0:05:26 — AI as a tool for thought (YouTube)
  • 0:06:42 — Leaving OpenAI: running toward something (YouTube)
  • 0:08:17 — The board crisis, in retrospect (YouTube)
  • 0:11:51 — Whose hand is on the dial: character vs. governance (YouTube)
  • 0:14:14 — What the moment demands of a leader (YouTube)
  • 0:15:48 — Building Thinking Machines: the tandem bike (YouTube)
  • 0:17:39 — The war for talent (YouTube)
  • 0:20:28 — Jobs, dystopia, and agency (YouTube)
  • 0:22:15 — Will humans always be in the loop? (YouTube)
  • 0:23:40 — Killer instinct and competition (YouTube)
  • 0:25:44 — The preview, and resisting short-term pressure (YouTube)
  • 0:27:16 — Success beyond wildest expectations (YouTube)

My Notes

  • New tools can change how we think. Positional notation didn’t just speed up arithmetic over Roman numerals, it changed what mathematics a person could attempt, and the idea that representational systems shape cognition runs from writing to Kenneth Iverson’s “notation as a tool of thought”. What she raises but doesn’t answer is whether AI tools are a notation-level shift that expands what we can think about, or an accelerant that speeds up the thinking we already do.

  • Institutional design over individual virtue. “Morality is not everything,” she says, pointing instead to decision-making structures, transparency, and governance, because “even people who are well-intentioned can make mistakes.” Good individual intentions don’t guarantee good outcomes at the organizational level, where morality is an emergent property of incentives and structure and can degrade even when everyone inside means well. That gap between personal ethics and what an institution produces is the failure mode Robert Jackall’s Moral Mazes [1] documents. It’s notable coming from a frontier-lab CEO, since the AI-governance conversation mostly fixates on founder character (“whose hand is on the dial”), which she’s arguing is the less durable lever.

  • Her focus on human agency lines up with the Pope’s. The tandem-bike image puts the person at the center of the design rather than efficiency. That is close to Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical on AI, which makes the dignity of the human person the measure for AI ahead of efficiency or profit.

  • “Human-in-the-loop leads to alignment” needs to be validated. She says collaboration gets you value-alignment “as a result of this approach.” Learning from humans in the loop isn’t new: RLHF is exactly that. But RLHF aligns a model to human intent, following instructions and preferences, which isn’t the same as aligning it to human values: a model can do what you asked and still optimize for something you don’t endorse. The signal differs in kind, and whether training to follow the former can lead to adherence to the latter needs further investigation.

  • Is humans-in-the-loop just a waypoint? She defends keeping humans in the loop in time-bound terms: “for as long as we can,” and making sure “this period” is meaningful. Asked directly whether humans might eventually leave the loop, she answers “it is possible.” So the position may be less “humans belong in the loop” than “removing them now would forfeit our chance to get the transition right.” That leaves open whether the destination is still full autonomy, approached more carefully. It’s the same question that runs through the automation-vs-augmentation debate.

Transcript

What’s here is the auto-generated transcript from the YouTube video, reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The dialog is verbatim in substance but lightly edited for readability — filler words and stutters removed, punctuation, capitalization, and paragraph breaks added (auto-captions ship without them). Nothing was paraphrased or reordered. Four editorial layers have been added:

  • Chapter outline. 14 chapters, each linking to its YouTube timestamp. The titles are editorial summaries of what’s being discussed, not verbatim quotes. The full outline is in the right-hand sidebar.
  • Inline hyperlinks. First mention of a salient person, company, or concept links to an authoritative source.
  • Bracketed expansions. Where an acronym appears without being spelled out in speech, the expansion is inserted in [square brackets] to mark it as editorial.
  • Editor’s notes in blue callout boxes flag dates and figures worth checking.

Speaker attribution was reconstructed from the captions’ speaker-change markers, so a stray line may be mislabeled. Obvious mishearings of names were corrected silently — ChatGPT, OpenAI, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, GPT-4o, o1 — and one content word was an inferred fix (nuances for the captions’ “neurons”).

0:00:00 — What interaction models are: continuous, not turn-based

Emily Chang: Let’s start with today and what you’re working on. You are building interaction models at Thinking Machines — models that you say keep humans in the loop. What exactly does that mean?

Mira Murati: We’ve been working for the past year and a half on the foundations of building a frontier AI lab, with the specific focus that we have. And the interaction models were a first look at our concentrated bet toward human-AI collaboration.

The reason why we even started Thinking Machines is because we wanted to build the frontier AI lab that’s really focused on the human-AI collaboration piece. That means a lot of things, and there are specific research bets that go into that, but we wanted to showcase our work in one of the first bets through the interaction models.

The interaction models are a new kind of model. If you consider the types of models that we work with today, they’re very turn-based. And so you talk, they talk, then they go off and think.

Once you’ve given a prompt on what it is that you want to do, while they’re thinking, it’s almost like they’re deaf and blind. They cannot perceive anything else about what’s going on. And then it’s your turn. And while you’re talking, they really cannot perceive anything about how you’re talking. It’s not happening in real time.

By contrast, our interactions with each other are very rich. There is a lot of information in our interactions — when we are silent, when we’re thinking, when we’re interrupting one another. And so interaction models are able to capture all of these nuances.

They’re not turn-based, they’re more like time-based interaction, where they’re continuously taking in audio, text, and video and continuously providing output. Now, we cut this up in chunks of 20 milliseconds.

And this enables you to actually catch these things like interruptions and simultaneous speech, and really create a rich, high-bandwidth interaction between humans and machines, which we think is critical to enable agency and to enable people to be more in this loop as we advance AI further and further.

0:02:45 — The bet: human-AI collaboration over pure autonomy

Emily Chang: You’re basically trying to build an AGI [artificial general intelligence] lab from scratch. You’ve got OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, all with a significant head start, all of them racing to build smarter models. What is the bet that you’re making that they aren’t, and what do you think they are underestimating?

Mira Murati: So first of all, I think advancing the frontier of AI is incredibly positive-sum, and there is plenty of space for many different perspectives and ways of developing the technology. I think plurality is good — having a plurality of perspectives, of ways of building technology, different products, is great for the world.

Now, this is a pretty hard thing to do, so I think that’s why we don’t actually have many players. The barrier to entry is incredibly high. But in terms of creating something differentiated, I do think there is plenty of room.

I have always been very passionate about advancing the frontier of AI systems, and I think there is a potential for so much transformation for civilization that comes from that. But it’s not a predestined outcome. The way that we go about building it and deploying the systems really matters. And an area where there is very little work that’s been done so far is bringing the machine intelligence closer to where the knowledge is.

What I mean by that is, there is one path of advancing frontier systems which is very autonomous and doesn’t rely too much on the messiness of reality, or the experience that humans have day-to-day — and that’s quite a fast way of advancing AI systems, very autonomously. Autonomy is definitely a part of it, and it’s a very important part. But a missing part, where we haven’t done much work, is really focusing on human intent, on the messiness of interaction, enabling people more, and conceptually building frontier systems more like tools for thought. I think the most advanced AI systems are the most incredible tools for thought that humanity can ever have.

0:05:26 — AI as a tool for thought

Emily Chang: And so how can this change the way that we think?

Mira Murati: We’re still thinking — but it’s changing the nature of thought, what we’re thinking about. And this part is familiar to us. Since the beginning of time, deep technologies have changed what we think about: language, writing, numerals. Imagine if you had to do multiplication with Roman numerals — it would be miserable. But we invented today’s numerals, and this enabled a whole area of mathematics. A child can do mathematics very quickly. So it enabled these very tangible new ways of thought. And I think this is the opportunity ahead of us — this possibility to expand what we think about, and have new tangible things that we think about. And this requires very intentional research work and product work in this direction.

0:06:42 — Leaving OpenAI: running toward something

Emily Chang: When I interviewed you, it was early 2023. ChatGPT had just changed everything, and you were CTO of OpenAI. A few folks I talked to said you basically ran the place — just saying. When you left to found Thinking Machines, were you running toward something or away from something?

Mira Murati: I most definitely was running toward something, once I figured out what that was. But I had an incredible experience at OpenAI. I was so incredibly lucky to work with some of the most dedicated and most talented people in the world, and that’s incredibly special. I’m very grateful for that experience.

Eventually I had my own view — a very strong view — of how I think this technology ought to be developed, and it’s very rare to start something from scratch once you have developed such a strong perspective on it. That’s a rare privilege to have. I think having a company like Thinking Machines gives us an opportunity to focus on where we have the highest conviction, and build and orient the entire company around that conviction.

0:08:17 — The board crisis, in retrospect

Emily Chang: Take me back to the board crisis of that year. Later that year, you testified under oath that you were worried OpenAI was at catastrophic risk of falling apart. You raised concerns about Sam Altman’s leadership. But in that moment, you had to act. Looking back, do you think you got that right?

Mira Murati: It was a very intense time, and a very complex situation. I’m sure many people have been in situations that felt impossible, where you have to make really hard calls very quickly.

There is a part of this complexity that wasn’t visible to the world — it appeared that it happened overnight, but to me it was years of thinking about the mission, the governance, how you build a team that can build durable, transformational technologies with that responsibility. There was a lot of complexity to the organization that had been there for years, and that we had thought about a lot.

This particular thing that happened, this acute moment — there was a lot of intensity to it, and very little time. When the board asked me for feedback, I shared feedback, and I stand by that. When they made the decision and asked me to step up as interim CEO, I did that. And when I realized that their decision was potentially catastrophic for the company and things would potentially fall apart, I felt like I had to act very quickly.

Even though on the surface it just looked very chaotic, at each point in time I felt very clear about what I had to do — because the thing that I cared the most about was the mission, the continuity of the mission, and the people and the team. This is not an abstract thing. It’s real people that I worked with for many years and cared very deeply about, and all of this was about to potentially implode.

So it was very clear to me what I had to do — to provide continuity, stability, and help bring Sam back, restore that, get the team in place to then deliver GPT-4o and o1. It was that principle that made it very clear to me what I had to do.

In retrospect, I think that I would have paused more on understanding the transition plan. With the benefit of hindsight, there wasn’t any transition plan, and there wasn’t much thought put into transparency — bringing the team along, providing continuity. In retrospect, I would have paused more on that.

Note

Editor’s note. The sequence: OpenAI’s board removed Sam Altman on November 17, 2023; Murati was named interim CEO; Altman was reinstated about five days later, and Murati returned to her role as CTO. Her “testified under oath” refers to deposition testimony in the litigation between Elon Musk and OpenAI. The two models she cites as what the team went on to deliver, GPT-4o and o1, were released in May and September 2024 respectively. Murati was OpenAI’s CTO from May 2022 until she left in September 2024.

Emily Chang: Interesting. Helen Toner, a former OpenAI board member, said: “Mira was waiting to see which way the wind would blow, and she didn’t realize she was the wind.” What do you think would have happened if you didn’t do what you did?

Mira Murati: I think quite likely OpenAI would have…

0:11:51 — Whose hand is on the dial: character vs. governance

Emily Chang: The case got thrown out on a technicality, so the court never decided whether the leaders of OpenAI breached their mission. How much does the character of the people building the most powerful technology in the world matter? Whose hand is on the dial?

Mira Murati: I think the integrity, character, and values of the people matter a lot, because there are a lot of decisions — micro-decisions — you have to make every day, and you have to trust your team that they’re making the right calls. There’s plenty of focus on that, and that’s great. Where there is less focus is the institutional design, decision-making, transparency — increasing the level of agency that people have to actually decide for themselves. So it doesn’t have to be an authority that says “this is safe, this is good, stamp of approval” — each person can weigh for themselves what works for them.

I think the way that we’re going about building AI systems today is very concentrated, and it’s partly the legacy way, because we didn’t have real-world data and experience. The only way to advance AI was in a silo, in a vacuum. But today is a different time to build, where we can actually learn a lot from the capabilities, tensions, and limitations in the real world, and use that data and information to steer the direction of research. This enables people to think for themselves.

Often people will ask me about ChatGPT and the impact of all of that. Of course it’s magnificent from a technology perspective, but I think the most important impact of ChatGPT in the public consciousness is that everyone kind of understands what it is by interacting with it, versus being told what AI can do and what its capabilities and limitations are.

0:14:14 — What the moment demands of a leader

Emily Chang: What do you think this moment demands of a leader, and should we trust the leaders in power right now?

Mira Murati: I think everyone should have the tools and information to make these decisions for themselves. Ideally, the structure of governance and decision-making should not hinge on one person. There should be checks and balances. I think it’s very important who is working on the systems, and the character of people. But I do think the conversation gets too wrapped up there, and not enough on thinking more broadly about checks and balances in the system — because even people who are well-intentioned can make mistakes, and they can misestimate the consequences of making a call.

So morality is not everything. You have to think about actual decision-making structures, and transparency, and governance. These are all complicated things. And to get as many people involved as possible, you actually have to share the knowledge. You have to share tools. This is part of the reason why we’ve taken a more open approach with our lab.

0:15:48 — Building Thinking Machines: the tandem bike

Emily Chang: So that was my next question — how is everything that you’ve learned shaping what you’re building at Thinking Machines, and how you’re building it, and the culture that you want to create?

Mira Murati: I have very high conviction that the way to continue building frontier AI systems is to bring people along, and to have humans in the loop. Actually, “having humans in the loop” doesn’t quite describe it, because it sounds like a checkpoint where we’re signing off on something and then you’re good to go.

It’s more like creating systems that are not just autonomously advancing and leaving civilization behind, but are more like a tandem bike where both people are pedaling. When you’re going up a hill, maybe whoever is stronger is pedaling harder, but both hands are on the wheel.

And that’s quite important, because that’s a different system — a system designed for collaboration. That’s what we’re trying to build with Thinking Machines.

I think it’s quite differentiated, and I hope that it will increase the level of agency that people have, and also help us steer the research direction toward creating outputs that are more value-aligned. So you also get alignment as a result of this approach, in addition to usefulness — actually creating technologies that are useful in the real world.

0:17:39 — The war for talent

Emily Chang: You’ve hired a lot of top talent. We’ve seen reports of nine-figure deals. There have also been some high-profile departures. How would you describe the war for talent? How brutal is it?

Mira Murati: It’s definitely a big part of building a frontier AI lab — having the right people, people who have the competence to do it but are also aligned with your overall mission, conviction, what you’re trying to achieve. I wouldn’t call it a war, because that might mean that the highest bidder wins. For the most part, people working in this field genuinely care about advancing the field. Now, it is an absolutely crazy time, and a lot of it is unprecedented. It’s incredibly intense to build a frontier AI lab from scratch during such competitive times. That leads to a lot of uncertainty, unpredictability, some of the volatility that we’ve seen. But when you’re trying to compress progress into such a short amount of time, things that happen in other startups over the course of ten years, five years — both good and bad — are going to happen in the course of a few months, or a year. Part of what we’re seeing is contextualized in that: just compressing the amount of progress that’s happening. And whenever you have something good, something bad will come with it, so you have to balance the two.

People leave for different reasons — maybe their passion evolves for what they want to work on. The high compensation numbers capture the imagination of people because obviously they’re very big, but I do think that for some of the most sought-after people, that’s not the main story.

There is a lot that goes on here, and it is very intense to build a company from scratch, let alone a frontier AI lab. So that’s part of the challenges and suffering of building a company and doing anything zero to one.

0:20:28 — Jobs, dystopia, and agency

Emily Chang: Dario Amodei has predicted mass white-collar job loss. Sam, though, recently walked back some of his predictions about a jobs apocalypse. Where do you think the industry is being too pessimistic, and too optimistic? What is Mira Murati’s vision for the future?

Mira Murati: Predicting a dystopia or a utopia, to me, feels very simplified, because the truth is we actually have a lot of agency in how we build this technology — in the tools that we’re building, in how we’re deploying it. It’s not a predestined outcome.

There are certainly risks; we all understand the potential for greatness that comes with building frontier AI systems, and that’s why we’re working on them. There’s been a lot of talk around the uncertainty and the downsides, and I agree with a lot of these risks. Perhaps where I might disagree, or take a different path, is that I think we have a lot of agency.

This period of time, where both humans and AI systems have their hands on the wheel and we can collaborate, is a very important time to get right. And the more that we can reduce the discontinuity that comes from new capabilities and huge changes in capabilities, the better. This is why we took this approach with Thinking Machines, and why the company exists.

Note

Editor’s note. Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, warned in May 2025 that AI could eliminate up to half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years and push unemployment to 10–20%. The “Sam” who walked back jobs-apocalypse predictions is Sam Altman of OpenAI.

0:22:15 — Will humans always be in the loop?

Emily Chang: So you say the goal is to keep humans in the loop. But is there ever a point where humans don’t need to be in the loop — and then what happens?

Mira Murati: It is possible. It’s more about aligning at that point — aligning intent and aligning values. But if you reduce progress to removing humans from this loop of development already now, then I see very little future possibility that we can get this right when AI systems are even more capable.

So I think the more likely path, and the more durable path, to advance AI in a way that enables and advances civilization, is by keeping humans in the loop for as long as we can, and really making sure that this period is actually very meaningful.

0:23:40 — Killer instinct and competition

Emily Chang: You’ve raised a lot of money. There are great expectations. If anything’s clear from the last few months in AI news, it’s that there’s some cutthroat competition out there. Do you think you have that killer instinct to take on OpenAI and Anthropic and Meta and Google and China and X — it’s a competitive world.

Mira Murati: It is extremely competitive. And yeah, we did raise a lot of money. We’re proud of that, but that’s not any big accomplishment — we didn’t set out to break some sort of record. It’s really what you do with that.

We’re not a normal company, and so you do need a lot of capital in order to build the infrastructure, the foundations of science, and all that’s required to actually have a claim at building frontier AI systems that are differentiated. So that part in itself is not unique.

In terms of killer instinct — that’s not really what motivates me. I think there’s actually a lot of room. We’re building a technology that has infinite potential, and it’s going to be hard to capture all of that potential. What motivates me is really capturing part of that potential — creating useful things in the world, bringing the technology into the world in a way that’s useful and increases human agency and advances our civilization.

There is healthy competition, and competition is good — it creates better products and better technologies for people. It raises the bar in many ways. I respect a lot of the companies that are doing this. But my motivation, day to day, when I wake up in the morning — I am not thinking about how…

Note

Editor’s note. Thinking Machines Lab raised about $2 billion in a seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz at a reported $12 billion valuation (July 2025), with investors including Nvidia, AMD, Cisco, and Jane Street — one of the largest seed rounds on record.

0:25:44 — The preview, and resisting short-term pressure

Emily Chang: You’ve said you plan to release a preview later this year. How far along are you? And with all of these other companies going public, do you think they’ll be distracted and you’ll have a little more room to run?

Mira Murati: We’re on our own path. Of course, the competition is fierce and we have to move quickly, but it’s important to balance that with durable, long-term progress. I care a lot about the decisions that we make today being good for our long-term success, and that’s something that I really try to instill in the team day to day. There is a lot of detail here with how you build the team, how you build the infrastructure, and really resisting the short-term pressures. In some cases you do have to embrace the pressure. But for us, this is just a first step — showcasing the interaction models and making it more concrete what it is that we think about and care about. I expect the next few months to show increased capabilities on the model side, more products in this direction, and to make it more obvious — really letting the technology and the products speak for themselves.

0:27:16 — Success beyond wildest expectations

Emily Chang: So a Thinking Machine succeeds beyond your wildest expectations. What exists then?

Mira Murati: It is extremely difficult to predict the future. But I’d say the most important thing would be to create a future where, regardless of how many hours of work we do day to day or week to week, we feel a sense of agency, a sense of dignity, and possibility about the future. I hope we’ll continue to advance the capabilities that will enable a lot of progress, and that we’ll do it in a way that will keep us hopeful and with a sense of possibility that we can drive about the future.

Emily Chang: Well, here’s to less impossibility, and…

References

Related posts

  • Emily Chang — Bloomberg journalist; the interviewer.
